ingredients.name: Freshly grated coconut
ingredients.notes: about 2 cups; or 85g dried grated coconut soaked in 120ml warm water for 20 minutes

ingredients.name: Shallots or red onion
ingredients.notes: small red onion or a handful of shallots, finely chopped

ingredients.name: Chilli powder
ingredients.notes: adjust to taste; the colour and heat of the sambol depend on this

ingredients.name: Maldive fish flakes
ingredients.notes: optional, for umami depth; omit for a vegan sambol

steps.instruction: If using dried grated coconut, mix with the warm water and soak for 20 minutes to rehydrate before use. Fresh coconut can be used straight away.
In a mortar and pestle (or bowl, if mixing by hand), grind or crush the shallots and garlic to a coarse paste.
Add the grated coconut, black pepper, chilli powder, and sugar to the onion-garlic paste. Mix or pound well, until the coconut takes on the colour of the chilli.
If using Maldive fish flakes, add them now and mix or grind through evenly.
Squeeze in the lime juice and add the salt. Mix or pound well, tasting and adjusting salt and lime as needed.
Serve immediately, traditionally alongside dhal curry, hoppers, string hoppers, kiribath, or bread.

notes: Pol sambol is considered the most essential, ever-present condiment in Sri Lankan cuisine -- eaten with virtually every meal, breakfast through dinner. It is distinguished from lunu miris (sl_017) by the inclusion of grated coconut as the bulk of the dish; lunu miris is a pure onion-chilli paste without coconut. Traditionally made with a stone mortar called a 'miris gala', though a mortar and pestle or even hand-mixing works well. Onion and garlic are not strictly necessary, but most home cooks consider them essential for freshness. This is a raw, no-cook dish meant to be eaten fresh; leftovers should be refrigerated and used within a day, as the lime juice and moisture in the coconut spoil quickly at room temperature.
